title: Few black students in school bands; black bands and education
summary: Most school musicians are white; Herman thinks successful black bands do not share experience, as do some white leaders like Buddy Rich.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Let's see. We mentioned about -- it was a little low in power, about the problems of recruiting black players.

Yeah. Well, I think one of the problems there, as I stated earlier, is the fact that at least in -- we have played so many schools in the last few years, and last year almost 80 percent of all our dates were in high schools and colleges. And, really, the percentage of black student players is very low in most areas of the country, and it doesn't seem to matter where.
No matter where, you mean, in the South or --

Yeah, you'll find some, but not in comparison to the other side of the picture. And I think this is really, truly unfortunate that they don't -- that there isn't more interest there, and I feel that it's to some degree due to
the fact that the black bands, the successful bands are not entering into the spirit of this imparting some part of your experience to someone else.
Have you discussed this with them at all?
No, I haven't, no. I haven't had the opportunity.
Uh-huh. I know Stan shares this view with you.

Yeah. But then, there are a lot of people, nonblacks, that never entered into the spirit of the educational process of trying to help, and I think that some of us, like Buddy Rich and many others, successful people, just don't want to know about all that.
They just ignore it, they say, 'Just let me play.'
Yeah, that's it, and they're -- which is -- I guess it is a little more comfortable, but I don't think we're handling the situation as to the future. If we don't enter into some of it.
You feel a responsibility toward that.
